The claim being held is structural: the kernel enumerates buses, and the
code that drives a device lives in ring 3 behind an IoMapping and an IOMMU
domain. That is what makes a userspace driver worth its cost, and it is the
kind of claim that decays one convenient access at a time.
Three kinds wear the same spelling in Rust and mean different things:
register  a device register -- MMIO or an x86 port. Reading one can have
side effects. Only these are confined by register_paths.
shared    RAM that a device or another process also reads: IOMMU tables,
virtio configuration space, the block and net rings.
memory    RAM that is volatile only so the compiler cannot elide an
access a check is making on purpose. Not about devices at all.
A script cannot tell them apart -- they are the same call -- so the entry
says which, and the diff that adds one is where that is argued. Calling a
register access 'memory' to get it past this gate is the thing the reviewer
//max_register_sites: The cap that binds. Register access is a fixed cost here: a console per
architecture, the x86 port primitives and their few users, the MMIO
accessors themselves, and PCI configuration space. 34 sites today; the
slack is for the boards this kernel has yet to boot on, not for a driver.
A new device is a ring-3 driver, and adds nothing here.
//register_paths: The sites ARCHITECTURE.md §1 and §7 permit a device register to be touched:
the MMU, traps, timers, interrupt controllers and serial writers under
arch/; the IOMMU units; PCI enumeration; the MMIO accessors; the shared
rings; the pre-MMU early console; and the framebuffer a panic draws on when
there is nothing left to trust. Every other path is a driver's job.

files.reason: The MMIO accessors themselves. Every memory-mapped register in the kernel goes through these six functions, which is the point: one place says what a device access is, and it is the one place a reviewer has to trust.
The x86 port primitives, inb/outb/inl/outl, and the asm that implements them. A port cannot be reached by a pointer; the instruction is the only spelling.
The PIT, calibrating the TSC at boot. A timer is an architectural service the scheduler needs before any driver could run, so it stays in the kernel; §1 permits timers.
The keyboard controller's reset pulse, the last resort when a triple fault is the alternative, and the 0x80 post code used as an I/O delay.
The 16550's data and status ports. The kernel's own console: a panic that cannot print is a panic nobody can read, so this cannot wait for a ring-3 driver.
The PL011's data and flag registers, the AArch64 and ARMv7-A console. As the 16550 above.
The STM32MP157's USART, the DK1's console. As the 16550 above.
The AArch64 console's register window, reached before the MMIO accessors are usable.

virtio configuration space in a function's BAR, read during enumeration and by the boot check that proves a translated domain works. §7 permits the kernel to enumerate; the driver that then runs the device is in ring 3.
Root and context table entries in RAM the VT-d unit walks itself. Volatile because the unit observes the write, not because the address is a register.
Stream table entries in RAM the SMMUv3 walks itself. As vtd.rs.

The GICv3 ITS's command queue and the LPI property table, in RAM the ITS and the redistributor read themselves. As smmuv3.rs: volatile because the interrupt controller observes the write, not because the address is a register.

The block ring's pages, which the ring-3 driver maps too. The protocol gives each byte one writer; volatile says the other side's writes are real. This is the seam working as designed, not a breach of it.
The net ring's pages. As block_ring.
Stage 6's boot checks: a page written and read back to prove a mapping, an alias, or a fault. Volatile so the compiler cannot decide the check proved itself.
The boot checks' probes: demand paging, W^X, the guard page, the kernel image's own bytes. Ordinary RAM, read for real because that is what is being proven.
Page table entries, through the direct map. The MMU walks them, which is why a write cannot be sunk; no device is involved.
Page table entries and physical bytes before the kernel's own mappings exist. As mm.rs, earlier.
Stage 4's cross-processor markers: a word one processor writes and another reads, which must not be held in a register.
The reverse map check's poison word, written through one mapping and read through another.
Reading a stack word while walking frames, where the frame may be corrupt and the read must not be reordered with the fault handling around it.
